source_note: Park & Newman (University of Michigan), 'A network-based ranking system for US college football', arXiv:physics/0505169v4 [physics.soc-ph], 31 Oct 2005 (Phys. Rev. E 72, 026136), 18 pages. One-parameter network centrality ranking for Division I-A college football (n=117 teams, 2004): schedule as directed graph (arrow winner->loser), asymmetric adjacency A_ij = times j beat i; direct wins = out-degree (Eq1), indirect wins = directed paths discounted by alpha per indirection level (Eq2); win score w_i = k_out_i + alpha sum A^T_ij w_j (Eq3), loss score l_i = k_in_i + alpha sum A_ij l_j (Eq4), total s_i = w_i - l_i ranks teams; vector resolvent w=(I-alpha A^T)^-1 k_out, l=(I-alpha A)^-1 k_in (Eq5/6) = generalization of Katz centrality. Strength of schedule automatic (beating strong team yields many indirect wins). Convergence alpha < lambda_max^-1 (largest eigenvalue); acyclic => no bound but real seasons always have loops; historical bound 0.2-0.3 (Table I). Retrodictive accuracy (fraction games won by higher-ranked team) ~80%, best at alpha ~ 0.8 lambda_max^-1. Outcome-free alpha: real networks fewer loops than random (strength variation), random-graph lambda_max = (<k^2>-<k>)/(2<k>) (Eq9, from Eq7 <k_in k_out>/<k_in> and Eq8 binomial degree split) ~20% larger than actual => alpha = 2<k>/(<k^2>-<k>) (Eq10) guarantees convergence, no outcome knowledge, near-optimal (2004 alpha=0.207). BCS comparison: 2004 top-25 correlation 0.90, top-5 agree >=3/5 each year 1998-2003, retrodictive parity; Auburn undefeated 3rd (concurs), Texas/California sides with computers; agreement not necessarily success. Non-football: bison dominance hierarchy (Lott 1979, 26 males), alpha=0.124, rank-breeding correlation 0.611, Lorenz/Gini. Single-parameter simplicity advantage; margin/home-field/season-progress as future edge-weight modifiers. Extracted faithfully (not a derivative summary). Equations 1-10 printed in math font that extracts garbled (null-glyph corruption + stacked fractions); reconstructed in labeled LaTeX from the unambiguous prose and flagged here and in assumptions. Domain football matches catalog (American college football network ranking). Directly isomorphic to GSE's pairwise-outcome schedule graph, opponent-quality-adjusted indirect-win credit, Katz-centrality ranking statistic, spectral convergence bound, and outcome-free pre-season discount calibration. No sportsbook lines/spreads/totals/implied odds in source or lifted into GSE.

primitives.name: Convergence requires alpha < lambda_max^-1; acyclic => lambda_max=0 (no bound); real seasons always have loops
primitives.verbatim_quote: there has never yet been a season for which there were no loops in the network
assumptions: The series in Eqs 3-4 converge only if alpha < lambda_max^-1 where lambda_max is the largest eigenvalue of A; if the network is acyclic (no loops A beats B beats C beats A) the largest eigenvalue is zero and there is no limit on alpha, but there has never yet been a season for which there were no loops in the network, so normally there is a finite upper bound on alpha.

layer2.mapping: The spectral-radius convergence bound is literally GSE's stability constraint on transitive-credit discount.

primitives.name: Historical alpha upper bound 0.2-0.3 (indirect win <= 1/5 to 1/3 of direct); Table I eigenvalues
primitives.verbatim_quote: Historically the values of this upper bound have been in the range 0.2 to 0.3
assumptions: Historically the values of this upper bound have been in the range 0.2 to 0.3 (Table I, 1998-2004 lambda_max from 3.39401 to 4.15120), so an indirect win cannot count for more than a fifth to a third of a direct win; but the number of indirect wins grows with indirection level, so they can still contribute substantially by sheer number, and alpha close to the upper bound gives roughly equal contributions from indirect wins at all distances.

layer2.mapping: The empirical spectral bound range is the same calibration window GSE uses for the discount parameter.

primitives.name: alpha=0 special case: only direct wins count, total score = win-loss differential
primitives.verbatim_quote: only direct wins count at all and the total score for a team is simply the win-loss differential
assumptions: A larger alpha places more weight on indirect wins relative to direct ones while a smaller one places more weight on direct wins; for the special case alpha=0 only direct wins count at all and the total score for a team is simply the win-loss differential, which correlates poorly with expert opinion due to strength-of-schedule variation.

layer2.mapping: The alpha=0 win-loss limit is literally GSE's naive-baseline anchor for the discount family.

primitives.name: Real schedules fewer loops than chance (strength variation => near-acyclic); random edges raise lambda_max
primitives.verbatim_quote: Real schedule networks have fewer loops than one would expect on the basis of chance, precisely because teams do vary in strength
assumptions: Real schedule networks have fewer loops than one would expect on the basis of chance, precisely because teams do vary in strength which gives rise to networks close to being acyclic; thus lambda_max is lower and the limit lambda_max^-1 higher in a real network than in a randomly-edged network (Monte Carlo randomization of edge directions consistently increases lambda_max), providing a safe practical upper bound on alpha without knowledge of game outcomes.

reasoning_traces.think: The retrocausal genealogy of this paper is the network-centrality turn in sports ranking. Juyong Park and M. E. J. Newman of the University of Michigan, posting to arXiv in 2005 as physics/0505169 and publishing in Physical Review E, start from the structural conflict that American college football wants a national championship but has no playoff, so ranking rests on win-loss records even though each team plays only a small fraction of eligible opponents, leaving the system underdetermined or contradictory. The work sits in the lineage of paired-comparison theory, the Perron-Frobenius ranking of Keener, the Katz status index and Taylor's influence structures, and the random-graph degree-distribution machinery of Newman, Strogatz and Watts, and it translates the folk transitive argument that a team which beat a team which beat another team is better than that other team into a precise centrality measure on the directed win-loss graph. The recursive theory of mind is the discounted path-count win and loss score. The schedule is a directed network with an arrow from winner to loser and an asymmetric adjacency matrix whose entry counts how many times one team beat another; direct wins are the out-degree, indirect wins at distance two are two-step paths, and higher-order indirect wins are longer paths discounted by a single parameter alpha per level of indirection. The win score is the out-degree plus alpha times the win scores of the teams beaten, the loss score is the symmetric quantity on the transpose, and the ranking statistic is their difference; in vector form these are resolvent inverses that generalize Katz centrality, so beating a strong team automatically confers many indirect wins and strength of schedule is built in rather than appended. Cross-layer veto adjudication is the convergence bound and the outcome-free choice of alpha. The path series converges only when alpha is below the inverse of the largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix, and because real seasons always contain loops there is a finite bound, historically between zero point two and zero point three. The best retrodictive accuracy — the fraction of games won by the higher-ranked team — sits near alpha equal to zero point eight of that bound, but computing the bound requires the whole season's outcomes, which is unavailable for weekly in-season standings. The authors' resolution is that real networks have fewer loops than random ones precisely because teams differ in strength, so the random-graph eigenvalue, computable from the games-played degree distribution alone as the mean-square minus mean degree over twice the mean degree, is about twenty percent larger than the true value and therefore lands alpha right in the optimal region without any knowledge of results. The implementation invariants map directly onto GSE. The directed winner-to-loser schedule graph is GSE's pairwise-outcome network representation; the discounted indirect-win credit is GSE's opponent-quality-adjusted strength kernel; the win-minus-loss Katz resolvent is GSE's network-centrality ranking statistic; the spectral convergence bound is GSE's stability constraint on transitive credit; and the closed-form outcome-free alpha is GSE's no-lookahead pre-season calibration rule that guarantees convergence while remaining near-optimal. The empirical validation and the cross-domain transfer give the method its credibility. Against the official Bowl Championship Series computer rankings the method achieves a rank correlation of zero point nine zero on the 2004 top twenty-five, agrees on at least three of the top five teams every year from 1998 to 2003, and matches the BCS retrodictive accuracy among the top teams, while siding with the computer polls against the human polls on the controversial California-versus-Texas case and concurring that undefeated Auburn was third. The same machinery applied to Lott's 1979 dominance hierarchy of twenty-six male American bison yields a rank-versus-breeding-success correlation of zero point six one one, visualized with a Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient, demonstrating that the ranking kernel is not football-specific but a general tool for pairwise comparison. The retrodictive-accuracy table makes the parity concrete: among the published top teams the method scores zero point eight one against the BCS zero point eight four in 2004 and zero point eight nine against zero point seven nine in 2002, and the alpha-zero limit reduces to the raw win-loss differential that everyone agrees on but that correlates poorly with expert opinion because it ignores strength of schedule, which is precisely the defect the indirect-win machinery repairs. The caveats and the design philosophy close the account. The authors are explicit that agreement with the official rankings is not necessarily a sign of success, since a genuinely better method must disagree somewhere, and they note that the retrodictive metric is computed on the final network and constrained to games among the top teams the BCS publishes. The method deliberately keeps a single parameter, treating margin of victory, home-field advantage and season progress as possible future edge-weight modifiers rather than complicating the present formulation, on the principle that simplicity reduces tuning while retaining an intuitive foundation and mathematical clarity. The invariant for GSE is to adopt the directed schedule graph, the discounted indirect-win Katz centrality, the win-minus-loss ranking statistic, the spectral convergence bound, and the outcome-free degree-moment alpha, while carrying the agreement-not-success caution, the final-network retrodictive scope, and the single-parameter parsimony as honest bounds on what the ranking can claim.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: Network-centrality turn in sports ranking. Juyong Park, M. E. J. Newman (University of Michigan Physics + Center for Study of Complex Systems); arXiv:physics/0505169v4 [physics.soc-ph] 31 Oct 2005; Phys Rev E 72, 026136. College football no playoff -> ranking from win-loss but each team plays small fraction of opponents -> underdetermined/contradictory; ~75% games intra-conference. Lineage: paired comparisons (David 1988), Keener 1993 Perron-Frobenius ranking, Katz 1953 status index, Taylor 1969 influence structures, Newman-Strogatz-Watts 2001 random graphs, Martinich 2002 retrodictive accuracy, BCS (Callagan-Mucha-Porter 2004). Folk transitive argument A beat B beat C => A better than C -> centrality on directed win-loss graph. NSF DMS-0405348 + McDonnell Foundation.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Directed network vertices=colleges, arrow winner->loser; A n x n real asymmetric (n=117 Div I-A 2004), A_ij=times j beat i (0/1/2). Eq1 direct wins_i=sum_j A_ji (out-degree); Eq2 distance-2 indirect=sum_jk A_kj A_ji; discount alpha per indirection level. Eq3 w_i=sum_j(1+alpha w_j)A_ji=k_out_i+alpha sum_j A^T_ij w_j; Eq4 l_i=k_in_i+alpha sum_j A_ij l_j; total s_i=w_i-l_i ranks. Eq5 w=k_out+alpha A^T.w, l=k_in+alpha A.l; Eq6 w=(I-alpha A^T)^-1 k_out, l=(I-alpha A)^-1 k_in (generalized Katz centrality). Convergence alpha<lambda_max^-1; acyclic lambda_max=0 (no bound) but real seasons always loops; bound 0.2-0.3 (Table I lambda_max 3.394-4.151). alpha=0 -> win-loss differential. Eq7 lambda_max=<k_in k_out>/<k_in>; Eq8 P(k_in=i,k_out=j)=2^-(i+j)C(i+j,i)p_{i+j}; Eq9 lambda_max=(<k^2>-<k>)/(2<k>); Eq10 alpha=2<k>/(<k^2>-<k>). Eqs 1-10 math-font (null-glyph) reconstructed.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Retrodictive accuracy = fraction games won by higher-ranked team (final network, Martinich 2002); ~80% broad alpha, best alpha~0.8 lambda_max^-1 (Fig3 1998-2004). Problem: lambda_max needs full season (post-season); want pre-season weekly standings. Real networks fewer loops than chance (strength variation -> near-acyclic); MC edge randomization raises lambda_max; random-graph lambda_max ~20% larger than actual -> bound ~0.8 of true = optimal region. Eq10 alpha outcome-free, guarantees convergence, near-optimal (2004 alpha=0.207 ~0.763 max; typically 0.7-0.85 max). BCS comparison: 2004 top-25 correlation 0.90; Pittsburgh+Florida outside top 25 (match all computers except Billingsley); Auburn undefeated 3rd (concurs); Texas/California method sides with computers; top-5 agree >=3/5 each year 1998-2003 (Table IV); retrodictive among top 25/15 comparable (Table V 2004 0.81 vs 0.84, 2002 0.89 vs 0.79). Agreement NOT necessarily success (better method must disagree). Non-football: bison dominance Lott 1979 26 males Montana, alpha=0.124, rank-breeding correlation 0.611, Lorenz curve/Gini. Simplicity single-parameter advantage; margin/home-field/season-progress as future edge-weight modifiers. Zero sportsbook lines lifted.

universal_lens: A network-physics study ranks Division I-A college football teams by representing the season schedule as a directed winner-to-loser graph and counting direct plus distance-discounted indirect wins and losses, yielding a win-minus-loss score that is a generalized Katz centrality and automatically encodes strength of schedule; the single discount parameter alpha is bounded by the inverse largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix for convergence, and the authors derive an outcome-free closed-form alpha from the games-played degree distribution that lands in the empirically optimal region, achieving 0.90 correlation with the BCS computer rankings and transferring to bison dominance hierarchies, while honestly noting that agreement with official rankings is not itself proof of superiority.
gsi_mapping: GSI treats directed schedule graph (arrow winner->loser, A_ij=times j beat i, n=117 Div I-A 2004); Eq1 direct wins out-degree sum_j A_ji, Eq2 distance-2 indirect sum_jk A_kj A_ji, alpha discount per indirection; Eq3 w_i=k_out_i+alpha sum A^T_ij w_j, Eq4 l_i=k_in_i+alpha sum A_ij l_j, s_i=w_i-l_i ranks; Eq5/6 resolvent w=(I-alpha A^T)^-1 k_out, l=(I-alpha A)^-1 k_in (generalized Katz); strength-of-schedule automatic; convergence alpha<lambda_max^-1 (acyclic lambda_max=0 no bound, real seasons always loops, bound 0.2-0.3 Table I); alpha=0 win-loss differential; retrodictive accuracy fraction games won by higher rank ~80% best alpha~0.8 lambda_max^-1; real networks fewer loops than chance (strength variation), random lambda_max ~20% larger; Eq7 lambda_max=<k_in k_out>/<k_in>, Eq8 binomial degree split, Eq9 lambda_max=(<k^2>-<k>)/(2<k>), Eq10 alpha=2<k>/(<k^2>-<k>) outcome-free near-optimal (2004 0.207); BCS 2004 top-25 correlation 0.90, top-5 >=3/5 agree 1998-2003, retrodictive parity, Auburn 3rd concurs, Texas/California sides computers, agreement not success; bison Lott 1979 26 males alpha 0.124 rank-breeding 0.611 Lorenz/Gini; single-parameter simplicity, margin/home/season edge-weight modifiers future; Eqs 1-10 math-font reconstructed.
gse_mapping: GSE lifts the directed winner-to-loser schedule graph as its pairwise-outcome network representation, the distance-discounted indirect-win count as its opponent-quality-adjusted strength-of-schedule credit kernel, the win-minus-loss Katz-centrality resolvent as its network ranking statistic, the spectral convergence bound alpha<lambda_max^-1 as its stability constraint on transitive credit, the retrodictive higher-rank-wins fraction as its validation metric, and the closed-form outcome-free degree-moment alpha as its no-lookahead pre-season discount calibration that guarantees convergence while staying near-optimal; treats the random-graph-versus-real loop-count difference as the insight that makes outcome-free calibration land in the optimal region, carries the agreement-with-official-not-success caution and the final-network retrodictive scope as honest bounds, and notes the single-parameter parsimony with margin-of-victory/home-field/season-progress available as future edge-weight modifiers; all outputs are network-centrality team rankings from win-loss records, never sportsbook lines.
